utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. I would first like to ask that everybody hears me. Are the interpreters all ready? Good morning to everyone. Does everybody hear me? Does the Prosecutor hear me? First I would ask the Prosecutors to identify themselves. I see there are some new faces here, some that I do know but I would like introductions in any case. Please introduce the Prosecutors, Mr Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Good morning, your Honours, good morning, counsel. I am assisted in this case, Mr President, by counsel to my left Ms Susan Somers, to my right Mr Ken Scott and to my far right Mr Patrick Lopez and the case manager, Mr President, is Alinde Verhaag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not sure I will remember all the names right away except, of course, my French colleague, to whom I say good morning, but I now turn to the Defence. We have the Defence attorney for Mr Kordic, who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good morning, I have the honour to present myself before this honourable Chamber. I am Mitko Naumovski, attorney at law from the attorney at law company Andres & Zogovic from Zagreb, Croatia. I am the Defence counsel for Mr Dario Kordic. Your Honour, I am kindly asking you for the permission to continue with further proceedings on Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible, to speak in Croatian. We have a booth which can interpret into that language, and you speak the language which you feel you are the most comfortable with for defending the interests of your colleague. Excuse me if I do not pronounce your name correctly. On your right, perhaps the gentleman could introduce himself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, good morning, colleagues. Let me present myself, my name is Bozidor Kovacic, I am an attorney at law from city of Rijeka in Croatia. I represent defendant Mr Mario Cerkez in this case and, of course, I join the request of my friend, even though I am speaking English relatively passable, I would like to have that opportunity to use Croatian language during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That causes no problems. This morning's hearing will have two parts, first there will be a public session for arguments, I believe that has already been referred to, that is for the request for pre-trial -- holding pre-trial motions in abeyance. My colleagues, Judge Riad and Judge Rodrigues have noted that what we had to do first -- this was what we had to do first in order to pass into a closed session to organise a status conference which I am sure will be fruitful and will provide concrete solutions to problems that we are faced with. I would now turn to Mr Harmon and remind him that on behalf of the Prosecutor's office, he filed a motion for holding -- to hold pre-trial motions in abeyance. I would first like to ask Mr Fourmy, who is the legal officer for this Chamber, to recall briefly the dates, or rather the number of preliminary motions, because there are a few of them, particularly the dates, so that we know what we are speaking about and at what point the Prosecutor's motion was filed, that is the motion to hold pre-trial motions in abeyance. Mr Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Thank you. As you know, in the case file there were several motions since October 1997, which first dealt with protection of victims and witnesses. Then there were several motions from the Defence dealing both with the accused Dario Kordic and the accused Mario Cerkez. These motions have several points in common, because they say that there is a defect in the form of the indictment that should not be admitted, so that parts of the indictment should be withdrawn which allege responsibility for not having punished. To withdraw several of the counts because they were not sufficiently argued as to the existence of an international conflict. There were motions about mens rea, inter alia command responsibility. Then there was a separate document dealing with withdrawal of the indictment and which concerned two of the co-accused of Dario Kordic. This was the end of December. We had a motion from the Defence representing Mario Cerkez requesting the extension of the time period for filing preliminary motions, a motion which the Chamber granted, and allowed these motions to be filed until 24th December 1997 -- 23rd December, excuse me. Then about two additional weeks in relation to the regular date when the time period would expire, and then there was a motion from the Prosecutor on 19th December 1997 for suspending the review of the preliminary motions to which the Defence answered on 28th December by letter and then a response from the Defence dated 14th January opposing this -- objecting to this request. Lastly, there was the Prosecutor's reply objecting to the objection of the Defence. That motion for suspending the review of the preliminary motions is the one which will be discussed in public this morning, your Honour, as you would like to organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have I made a mistake about the initial appearance which is 8th October 1997 and that therefore the 60 days for filing preliminary motions would be concluded on 8th December? But it was 4th December that all of these Defence motions were filed, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were several days difference according to whether one refers to the request filed on behalf of Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez, but these are the dates that should be kept. Everything depends upon the faxing dates, that is the dates that they were officially registered by the Registry. Yes, in fact, it was 8th December 1997 and 23rd December which was the only one from Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we agree then. So we could say that practically speaking, so we can know what we are talking about today, since the initial hearing of 8th October, the 60 day time period has elapsed since the end of that period which, according to its right, the Defence filed preliminary motions which you have just mentioned with an extension relating to Mario Cerkez and since that time, we have received nothing in the case file. As regards the judges, today we rendered a decision about a request which is still confidential and I will not mention it. That is where we are and we must keep in mind dates from 19th November 1995 and the initial appearance, further to the arrival of the two accused in The Hague, dates from 8th December 1997, and then all of these motions were filed just about at the end of the 60 day period for one of the accused as well as for the other, who had the time period extended, and that the Prosecution then presented its request for holding pre-trial motions in abeyance. Having said this, having recalled this both for my colleagues, who I am sure know this, but for the Prosecution and Defence as well, I believe that we can now give the floor to Mr Harmon. I think he will be the one who will speak for the Office of the Prosecutor, so that he can elaborate on his motion. Mr Prosecutor, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, I will not be arguing the motion, my colleague Susan Somers will be arguing the motion on behalf of the Prosecutor's Office. I would just like to say, however, at the outset, that when the accused made their initial appearance and after their initial appearance, I personally had a meeting with Mr Naumovski and Mr Andres and another gentleman who was a lawyer from the United States who was considering coming into the case and it was after that initial appearance that Mr Naumovski and I and counsel discussed the possibility of suspending the filing of motions, until after the indictment itself had been amended, so against that backdrop, Mr President, you should be aware that then motions were filed, but there were preliminary discussions that lasted over an hour in which we discussed the possibility of holding all motions in abeyance. Now, Mr President, if I may turn to my colleague, Ms Somers, she will address the Chamber in respect of this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Proceed, please, Ms Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours and learned counsel. Just as an additional word, we were a little surprised to receive the opposition to the motion, given the backdrop of discussions and including some correspondence sent by Mr Harmon to which I was party or privy to Mr Kovacic, indicating the very high likelihood of amendment, so from the inception, amendment has been in the discussion and as Mr Harmon indicated, it was clearly contemplated by the parties at the meeting with Mr Kendall and the two counsel for Mr Kordic. We did file yesterday, and I do not know if the court has had an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just one moment please, I am going to interrupt you. I do not usually interrupt, but excuse me at this time. These conversations that Mr Harmon has alluded to, what date was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe it was December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I need the exact date because we are starting with 19th December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: October 21st is when the meeting took place between Mr Naumovski, Mr Andres and Mr Kendall, as well as Mr Harmon and Mr Bowers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 21st October, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In as much as we filed only yesterday the response to counsel's opposition, I would like to just have a chance to itemise the points in that response. Because Mr Kordic and Mr Cerkez were part of an original indictment with a number of co-accused, and because of the piecemeal nature of the surrender, there has been quite a bit of activity in trying to accommodate the number of trials that have been generated out of said piecemeal surrender. As of October 1997, although the case clearly was in the hands of the Prosecutor, very few officers were actively -- will actively investigate fugitive cases and these individuals were in fact fugitives. Although the point is raised that we have had the case two years -- that is evident, we have had the case two years, but active reinvestigation will only commence upon surrender or arrest. Our position is that because we have had a chance to discuss in both informal and in formal initial appearances matters concerning how we intend to progress that there was really no problem, and that there is certainly no prejudice in that the amount of time which ultimately we are trying to ask the court to grant us for reindictment is not excessive given the very complex nature of this case. Please be on notice that it is a very complex case. We anticipate multiple witness repetition unfortunately, because of the piecemeal way things have been handled with the surrender, and we are now taking an opportunity to re-evaluate and re-examine as we are mandated to do the evidence and investigative materials that we had derived in 1995 and prior to that time. As this court knows, and perhaps it was not highlighted in the previous enumeration of events, also on 19th December this honourable court granted the Prosecutor's motion to withdraw indictments as to two of the co-accused in this case, Mr Santic and Mr Skopljak, and therefore only as of 19th December did the Prosecutor's Office have a clear identifiable pool of who the accused in this case would be. It would not have been really known against whom we would file an amended indictment and I want to emphasise this fact. The court also was made aware at the time that we filed the motion to withdraw, which this court granted, that we would be -- we very diligently undertook a reinvestigation quickly. We are very mindful of the obligations for a fair trial, both for the Defence and the Prosecution. No one wants to prejudice either side, and we undertook very deliberately and quickly to assess the character and quality of the evidence, and having done so, we elected to file our motion to withdraw those two indictments, as well as one in another sister case, as it were. Therefore we have now turned our full attention, as we tried to from the outset of the surrender, to these two accused and are working very diligently to reassess, to check which witnesses are still available who were available years ago. Some will not be and, of course, new witnesses have come into the picture. We have learned a considerable amount since this original indictment was filed. I think that the complexity of the case which will be borne out over the course of time will certainly indicate that we are trying to be very reasonable in our approach to this motion. We saw it as essentially unfair and not in the interests of either judicial or legal economy to litigate twice motions which the second time round may not be applicable if we amend the indictment in such a way that these motions do not touch the issues. Therefore it seemed natural, logical and efficient, as well as fair, to wait, to hold things in abeyance, as was discussed earlier. I see no issue of prejudice from the standpoint of preparation. The motions which were submitted resemble very much other motions which have been before this court in the sister case of Blaskic, and many of the issues have already been decided. However, because we will have potentially a different approach to the indictment, it would just seem a better way to wait the limited amount of time we are requesting and then proceed on a normal scheduling order. There was a clear indication by Mr Kordic's counsel that suspending a scheduling order would be an appropriate way to handle things. We, of course, agreed. We never opposed the request for the extension by Mr Cerkez's lawyer; to the contrary, we had no problem with it whatsoever and as soon as the court granted the motions to withdraw the indictments on Messrs Santic and Skopljak Mr Harmon filed immediately the motion to hold in abeyance, since we at that point knew with whom we would be dealing. We did not even wait for the Registry. Because of the Christmas holiday issue, I personally faxed those motions to counsel, so they would have the benefit, so if that weekend were critical to Mr Cerkez's lawyer, he would know and would perhaps make an appropriate request to the court. Therefore, under all the circumstances of our dealings with opposing counsel and given the nature of how these individuals came before the court and what we have been able to accomplish very quickly to hone in on who will be the accused, we asked this court please to grant our motion to hold in abeyance once it has been determined the date for filing a new amendment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, I now turn to Defence counsel. Mr Naumovski or Mr Kovacic, I do not know if either of you wishes to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I would like to say this is a motion that was submitted by both accused who find themselves in the same situation. The explanation is in two parts. First I will start and then my colleague Kovacic will go on. Allow me to reply to the introductory remarks made by my learned colleague just now. It is true that the Defence of Dario Kordic did discuss at a single occasion on 21st October 1997. During that first conversation, the Defence wanted to prove that during the whole proceedings, if that is made possible, we are going to be as co-operative as we can, obviously bearing in mind the interest of our defendant Mr Dario Kordic. Our acceptance to be very co-operative, we stand by it today as well and we are going to do our utmost in order to achieve that. That does not mean that the Defence needs to wait for a limitless amount of time without having been given the indications when we will be able to do something. So one thing is to say that we are going to co-operate and quite a different matter not to know for how long we will have to wait, and keeping our defendant waiting without him knowing for how long. That is precisely why the Defence asked the Prosecution to say when and if they were going to amend the indictment, so that the Defence could prepare for its case. That is why it is surprising to us that in the reply we received yesterday, surprise is expressed as to our behaviour when we were so very co-operative from the beginning. The Defence of Mr Kordic sticks entirely to our objection to the motion about the abeyance, but we have to give some additional elements. From the motion filed on 19th December 1997 and also in the response to our response of 28th January 1998, and also from what we have heard from our learned colleague this morning, there is one conclusion that we can see, that the real need for this additional time is the need to make more investigations. Were it not so, then if we see the separation from the cases concerning Blaskic and Aleksovski and the withdrawal of the charges concerning Santic and Skopljak, they would need only a few days to reorganise the indictment, and also it proves to another fact which is an even more important one, that is that the Prosecution is not ready to proceed to trial. In the response given on 6th January 1998, the Prosecution ask for a deadline until 2nd March 1998 for the indictment to be amended. We consider that such a long delay should not be granted because in that case, the defendants' right to a quick trial would not be permitted. We cannot stop the proceedings for the moment just because of this indictment, or we cannot accept such long delays. In case that happened, then the Prosecutor would simply give a de facto -- be given de facto control over the case. It is true that the accused surrendered at different times during a two year period, which resulted in separate cases, but from the viewpoint of the Defence of Mr Kordic, we would like to point out that that very fact should not in any case have negative consequences on the accused that are present here. Every defendant responds only for their own acts, they respond individually, according to the criteria of subjective guilt. Within that context, to try and call for an economical proceedings is something that should not be called upon. Your Honours, both accused have surrendered only to the International Tribunal out of their own free will, and not to the Prosecution, not only because the promises were given that the trial will take place quickly, but also for the regularity of the proceedings. The defendants have got the right to a quick and fair trial, and that is precisely what the Prosecution is opposing at the moment. I also have to say that the Defence cannot accept at all, and I might even say that we do not consider it fair, when the Prosecution states that in the case Prosecution versus Blaskic that the motions had been filed and that there were decisions that were already made, the rulings were given according to these motions, and there is obviously some similarity with the motions filed in this case; activities linked to rulings and decisions in a different case cannot influence the position of this particular accused because the case is different. That is why we consider that the Tribunal should set the date for the hearing about the motions filed by the Defence because it is only up to the Prosecution to say whether and how they are going to accept or refuse our requests. That is why, your Honours, we would like to propose that the Prosecution's request be not granted, because it is unfounded, and that you set a date for a hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Since your colleague indicated that you would be dividing the work, that you would be splitting the work, you may then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: First I would like to say that I fully join the opinion of my distinguished colleague, but, however, I would like to add only a couple of points, and I will try to be very brief. First, what we just have heard from the Prosecutor's desk this morning. I think that the bottom line of that message was that the Prosecutor's Office told us once again, "we are not ready to go to the trial", in spite of the fact that the indictment was brought on November 2nd or 5th 1995. More than two years have passed, and the Prosecutor is telling us again, "we are not ready to go into the trial". Also the other message was that when the Prosecutor decided to give up on the accused from the same case in the same indictment, Santic and Skopljak, they are now basically trying to capitalise on their mistakes, on their errors. We all know why and based on what material formerly accused Santic and Skopljak were here in The Hague and suddenly they are out of the case. Obviously the indictment was not ready at the time when it was brought and that is the core of the problem we are today discussing. I would also like to add that in all criminal systems in all countries, either continental or Anglo-Saxon system, there is a presumption that as soon as the Prosecutor brought the indictment, he is ready to go to the courtroom. It is obvious that the Prosecutor should do so, because at that very moment when the indictment is brought, we are entering the area of the rights of the accused person, particularly when we are having a case where custody or detention of the defendant is obligatory. So one should be very careful when bringing up the indictment. One should be sure that there is at least prima facie a case. However, if the Prosecutor wished to amend the indictment, he can do so, he is entitled to do so at each phase of the trial, in pre-trial phases and during the trial; but he is not entitled to ask a court to stop with the proceedings, which necessarily means delay, while he is considering to amend the indictment. We have been told from the very beginning of this case, shortly after the defendants voluntarily appeared before this court, that the Prosecutor would amend the indictment. However, nothing happened, and now after more than three months, almost three months, the Prosecutor is still telling us, "we will amend the indictment". We will be happy to see that. Indeed, I would refer only to the one small detail. In an effort to save time, to try to co-ordinate, to try to work together, among other things, I send a letter to the Prosecutor on 17th November. A couple of issues were discussed. Among other things, I ask the Prosecutor once again about amendment of the indictment. I told them that there is obviously something in the process, that he obviously will seek an amended indictment, and I ask him, I will read that sentence: "If that presumption is correct, I request that amendment is done as soon as possible in order to ensure that the charges are identified promptly so that I may proceed with preparation of defence. It is obvious that unjustifiable delay in amending the indictment would cause hardship for the Defence, not to mention the defendant's right to a speedy trial." Soon I received an answer on November 28th, where the Prosecutor once again stated and confirmed his position. Shortly he said: "The Prosecutor merely wishes to emphasise that it is the prerogative of the Prosecutor to amend an existing indictment at either pre-trial or after the trial has commenced", et cetera. So I think there is no dispute on the fact that the Prosecutor very well knows for a long time that there is a need to amend the indictment. We cannot accept that this fact influences on the position of the defendants. Their basic rights in this procedure is expeditious and fair trial. In this phase of the trial, I mean in the pre-trial phase, the point is -- the accent is on the fast, speedy trial. In this phase of the trial, we can lose, Defence may lose, two, months, five months, six months, eight months, ten months, so each party should be very disciplined in planning what to do and how to proceed, because in this case we have defendants in custody and we have to act accordingly. For that reason, my final proposal is the same as of my distinguished colleague, that the motion of the Prosecutor to suspend the proceedings should be denied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Office of the Prosecutor wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you for the opportunity. Your Honours, learned counsel, a few points. First of all, I think that, and not necessarily in any type of self-serving statement, but I think good faith has very much been the byword of the behaviour of the Prosecutor in this entire set of proceedings, and in terms of having taken no action on the indictment, I would have to indicate that having withdrawn the indictment as to two individuals in a jointly charged instrument I think is a significant advancement for this courtroom and for both sides. In terms of the amount of time, again I think that no one should profit by deliberate dilatory action and although surrender did occur, it occurred two years after a notice of the existence of the indictment. The standard that has been discussed was based on Rule 47 which clearly contemplated at that time a much lower level of proof. As the court may remember, in the issue of our seeking withdrawal of the earlier indictments, we conceded a prima facie case clearly was there. However, to proceed to trial we need to have the proper standard met and we are diligently working on making sure that the evidence we have meets that standard. I think expeditiousness cannot exist in a vacuum and in this type of case, with its complexity and with its due speed with which we have proceeded thus far, given all circumstances, the balance between fairness and expeditiousness must be very carefully looked at and this court has always at all times done so. To hurry would not necessarily mean to be fair, so we ask that the court grant our motion so both sides have the fairness that so properly belongs in a case this complicated. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I turn to my colleagues, perhaps my colleague Judge Riad or Judge Rodrigues have questions. I myself do have some comments that I would like to make. I am going to turn to the Prosecution who is making this request. The dates do not really speak highly for the Prosecutor, that is the least one can say, since the accused have been here since October. I think we have to start from legal perspectives and application of the Rules which bind both of us. It is true that the rights of the Prosecutor are always connected with the indictment, but the first question that I ask is to the representative of the Prosecutor who has just spoken and who has just said that the level of proof has changed over the last two years in relation to the indictment. If you wish to answer me you may, but the judges confirmed indictments two years ago, they continue to do so. I do not think there are any particular guidelines that would have been given by the plenary session. It is true, according to the temperaments of the different judges and depending on their different legal cultures, the level of presumption is rather high, I do agree. It is true that those who work in continental law have a level of presumption that is broader than the prima facie level that one finds among legal specialists of the commonwealth system. I do not know who confirmed this indictment, but you do know, Ms Somers, that there are not many civil lawyers in the first group of judges at this Tribunal. This is my first comment and I would ask that you respond to that. My second comment, we are looking at this problem, which is that if we were to hold in abeyance the preliminary motions, you would modify or amend the indictment. According to that reasoning, the indictment can be amended during the trial and we agree with that, but for you to ask for this abeyance it means that you intend to make substantial amendments to the indictment and the fact that Santic and Skopljak are no longer being prosecuted -- and what has struck me is that this argument has been used by both sides, really does not convince me very much, because you have withdrawn the Prosecution against two of the accused but nonetheless the indictment remains the same. I would go even further than that. I would remind you that the indictment was the same originally insofar as it included Tihomir Blaskic and Aleksovski. I do have to say this, because this is a public hearing, that if there is an indictment that should be ready, that is the one, because in the end, both trials have begun, one in June and the other -- I turn to my colleague on my left, Judge Rodrigues, who is the presiding judge of that Trial Chamber and who is hearing the Aleksovski case, so I do have to say that at least from the point of view of legal appearance, at least from that appearance, we are getting to the substance of this matter; if there is an indictment that has to be ready, it is the one that involves two of the co-accused whose trial has begun. Therefore the argument of Skopljak is not particularly very convincing. My third question, Ms Somers, has to do with the additional investigations. Here too we find an indictment which goes back two years. Many problems are common to both the trials. I know that there are walls separating both of them, both the trials, and the Defence has just said that, that these are different defendants, they are not all the same, and I know we are talking about individual criminal responsibility and you are dealing now with professional judges who understand that fact very well. Nonetheless, as regards the basis upon which we are working now, that is the indictment, we know that the facts are the same, the acts are the same. There were atrocities that were committed on some of the territory of Central Bosnia. As regards these three points, I would like to have some comments, responses that is. The fourth point has to do with the schedule. Although I can understand that a significant amendment of the indictment will cause further delays, I do understand that, but I have two other questions which then arise. What are the significant amendments to the indictment, and I do not want to hide the fact from you that I am beginning to worry a bit. Yesterday two of the judges in this Chamber presided over an initial appearance of another accused who has nothing to do with the problems of Central Bosnia and we were told there would be amendment to the indictment. We were also told during another trial -- is there a kind of tornado going through the Prosecutor's Office which is changing all of the indictments? If that is so, then the judges at least should know. Is there a policy change and as regards our trial, I would like to know whether these are significant and substantial amendments, you must have an idea by now. I am not going to ask you to argue on that, Ms Somers, because if the Trial Chamber accepted the amendment to the indictment then you would make those amendments in proper time. They would have to be significant amendments. If it just has to do with defects in the form of the indictment, it would be a matter of responding to the Defence motion who filed a preliminary motion on the defects of the form of the indictment. Everything leads me to think it is not a simple formal amendment to the indictment, otherwise you would have responded to the preliminary motion of the Defence, but that we are talking about significant amendment and if that is the case, one is entitled to wonder why the Office of the Prosecutor for the last two years now was not able to realise that in this case the date the accused would be present in this courtroom significant amendments would be made to the indictment. My last question, which I think is the fifth , is to know why there are additional investigations in a case file which should more or less be prepared now. I understand that you have to locate the witnesses again. In all of the cases, when the witnesses come in a year or two years after the indictment, I understand that they have to be found or new witnesses must be located, but now you are talking about additional investigation. Are we talking about something significant or not so significant? The Trial Chamber wants to know this, wants to have an answer before it grants or does not grant the motion to hold in abeyance the pre-trial motions. I do not know whether Ms Somers or Mr Harmon will answer my question, but I would like one of you to answer them please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I hope I have properly noted the order of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One moment, please. (Pause). I needed to consult my colleagues. Ms Somers, would you please respond to the five questions that I have asked on my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I think the level of proof as we interpret it in Rule 47 has typically contemplated additional investigation even once an accused comes into custody and to bring it up to the trial standard is our goal, so that we can actually start. Clearly a prima facie case was set forth and as we have interpreted it, it requires some additional shoring up. The similarity of some of the charges is another point that was raised by the court with the Blaskic case, has merit. However, there are substantial differences that at this point we are trying to clarify as to the extent of the contemplated changes. There are currently witnesses who were unavailable in the past who are available now, who will probably help us or will help us clarify types of lines of authority that become issues in this type of case, and we need -- we have needed and we continue to need the time we request in order to perfect our assessment of this issue. I think the other point was the additional investigation; I do not know it would be considered a separate investigation, but it is to make sure that upon which we predicated the case initially is sound and that anything new that has come into our possession is integrated into the indictment as we would like to present to the court. I hope I have touched the issues, I do not know if I jotted them down correctly. If I need to answer anything more, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for having answered. If you did answer correctly, you will see it in the decision we will render. Turning to the Defence, do you have any additional comments you would like to make in relation to this discussion between the judges and the Office of the Prosecutor. Would you like to make any additional comments? Mr Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps literally only one or two words, I really would not like to waste our time. The point is that the Prosecutor is insisting on new investigation, additional investigation. They should consider a new indictment, they should consider giving up this indictment. We cannot keep in detention, in custody, the defendants and going for new investigation. That is impossible. That is like Vishinski in Soviet Union in 1923. We know there is something but we do not know actually what there is. Of course I am trying to emphasise the thing, but it should be carefully considered, are we talking about new indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not authorise you to -- I cannot, neither myself nor my colleagues, in this International Tribunal which was created by the United Nations, I cannot permit you to refer to a trial which everybody knows was a trial which was not fair, which was not rapid and I ask you to withdraw this statement in reference to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour I, of course, withdraw it. That was not really my intention. My intention was merely to point out that sometimes the Prosecutor does things in a different way to what is expected. I am just stressing that we should be very careful in how far are we going in amended indictment, what are we really talking about? Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I had thought no one wanted to say anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honour, just a brief comment. I second my colleague Kovacic that in essence the Prosecution, as was pointed out, have to start a new investigation rather than expand on an already existing one. This I gleaned from a detail that emerged when you asked the small question, when you asked about the changes, were there any essential changes to be made. The distinguished colleague who did not need to say this today, but needed to point out the direction in which they would go, so with this avoidance of that issue, we could glean that we would know about where this indictment is going, based on this investigation that is yet to proceed. So this is the only further point that I wanted to make, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, the discussion about this motion is now almost completed, but I would like to go forward and make a practical comment. Do you believe, Ms Somers, that you will be prepared with the amendment to the indictment by what date? When we look at all that has been said, when do you think you will be able to present these amendments, if they are granted to you by the Trial Chamber? How long would it take you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we set forth in our reply yesterday that we are seeking to 2nd March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I read that. I am saying in light of what has been said right here, let me remind you that this is now the end of January and that since November, you have been aware that you knew you were going to make a motion permitting you to make substantial amendments to the indictment. I allow myself to say that Mr Cerkez and Mr Kordic have been here since October. Perhaps you cannot answer this question right now, so you remain with your request for 2nd March, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We would respectfully ask the court to consider that date, we think it should help us substantially in doing the best job we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me once again turn to my colleagues to ask them whether they have any additional comments they would like to make. I believe there is no reason to speak any further about the presentation of this motion. We will now take a few minute break, long enough in order for us to have a closed session status conference, which will allow us to settle some practical questions relating to the organisation of the trial. (10.35 am)
